lines.text: Every great fast bowler spends years learning one thing.
This one learned it in six hours.
And nobody taught it a thing.
This is the story of how it learned, how it cheated, and how it finally earned its wickets.
Bowling looks simple. Run in, let go.
But every ball is four decisions. How fast, how full, what line, and which way it swings.
Then physics takes over. Gravity pulls it down, the air slows it, the seam makes it swing, and the pitch decides how it bounces.
And you never quite hit your mark. A tiny error at release becomes a big miss at the other end.
My bowler has that problem too. Every ball gets a random wobble, so it can't rely on perfect aim.
My simulator models all of it, stepping each ball's flight every two milliseconds, from release to the stumps.
Then, there's the batter.
It faces three of them. Each one has strengths, a hidden weakness, and a mind of their own.
The Slogger. Aggression, ninety four out of a hundred. Anything full or short goes over the ropes.
His weaknesses: the yorker on the stumps, and the slower ball he swings at too early.
The Technician is the opposite. Skill, ninety one. He leaves everything wide and blocks everything straight.
One flaw. A good length ball on fourth stump that moves away late. That one, he edges.
And the Tailender. Brave, not skilled. He hops around against the short ball, and a full, straight one can sneak through.
None of them is a fixed target. Each one tracks what you've been bowling. Length, line, movement, pace.
Repeat yourself and their confidence climbs, and a confident batter is much harder to get out.
Surprise them, and you're in the game. Real batters work the same way.
And every over, each batter is varied a little, so the bowler never faces exactly the same player twice.
The bowler is a neural network. Eighteen inputs: which batter, his confidence, the score in the over, and the last two balls.
Two layers of twenty four neurons. Four outputs. One thousand, one hundred and fifty six numbers in total.
No rules of cricket are written anywhere. Whatever it learns, it learns by playing.
Instead of teaching it, I let it evolve.
Generation zero is chaos. Against the Slogger, random bowling goes for more than thirteen runs an over.
A hundred and ninety two random brains each bowl forty eight overs.
The best eight go straight through. The rest of the next generation is bred from the winners, by mixing two parents and adding small mutations.
Repeat that fifteen hundred times, and you've bowled about eighty three million deliveries.
Watch a whole generation bowl at once. In generation one, the balls land everywhere. The lengths are spread across almost three metres.
By generation fifty, they've found the stumps. By five hundred, the swarm is almost a single stream.
By the end, the spread of lengths has shrunk to about half a metre, and the spread of speeds from six kilometres an hour to one.
And every champion has a family tree. The final one was born in generation fourteen twenty five. Follow its parents back, generation by generation, and you reach a random brain at generation zero.
Version one learned fast. Too fast.
When I watched what it was bowling, it was doing one thing. Bouncer. Yorker. Bouncer. Yorker.
A hundred and fifteen kilometres an hour, then a hundred and fifty. Nothing in between.
Half of all its balls were bouncers. Three an over, which is illegal in real cricket.
The reason was my batter model. My batters judged surprise only by how far a ball was from what they expected.
So swinging between two extremes was always the most surprising thing it could do.
The AI didn't learn cricket. It found a bug in my world, and farmed it.
This has a name in AI research. Reward hacking. You get exactly what you asked for, not what you meant.
So I fixed the world, not the bowler.
The batters now remember the last two balls and spot patterns. Run that bouncer yorker routine, and they've read it by the fourth ball.
And a surprise only works once. A shock ball takes a wicket more than a quarter of the time on the first ball of an over. By the sixth, it's down to two percent.
Bouncers above the shoulder are capped at two an over, like the real laws.
Then I threw the old brains away, and started from nothing.
Fifteen hundred generations later, every ball lands where it means to. Now, the duel.
First, the Technician. Good length, fourth stump. Blocked.
Again. He's getting comfortable. His confidence is rising.
Same length again. But this one moves late.
Edged. Caught behind.
The Slogger is dangerous. Two dots, then he cuts loose. Four. Four. Four.
His confidence is the highest it's been all over. He's waiting for the full toss.
The bowler doesn't give it to him. Full, straight, fast. Bowled.
Against the Tailender, the obvious plan is to bounce him. It doesn't. Full, straight, fast.
Trapped in front. Out, L B W.
It isn't unbeatable. The Slogger still scores almost six an over.
But it takes a wicket nearly every other over against him, and gives the Technician barely one run an over.
Watch the brain cam. Every ball, you can see which inputs it's reading.
The decision map shows how its plan shifts as the batter's confidence changes.
One habit it never outgrew. It always swings the ball away. Outswing is the classic fast bowler's weapon, so it's a good habit. But it's a habit, not a choice.
Before training, I wrote an expert plan for each batter by hand, the way a coach would.
Against the Tailender, my plan used both legal bouncers, then yorkers. The AI threw the bouncers away completely, and still did better.
And against the Technician, the single most dangerous ball is a yorker. But the AI bowls good length nearly three quarters of the time, because it plays the whole over, not one ball.
So how good is it? Random bowling scores zero. A hand written expert plan, designed for each batter, scores one.
The final brain scores one point two five, one point one six, and one point one eight. It beats the expert against all three.
The cheater, retested under the fair rules, scores around point six.
It isn't real cricket. It's a simulation, and the batters are models I designed. The bowler can only be as clever as the world it lives in.
But that's also the exciting part. Give it a better world, with real batters and real data, and the same idea could find the plan against anyone.
That's what I'm building next.
No coaching. No examples. Just a reward, a world that wouldn't let it cheat, and evolution.
This is the machine that learned to bowl.
